This dual pathway synergistically accelerates apoptosis of CD4⁺ T cells, impairing tumor immunosurveillance and promoting a microenvironment conducive to hepatocarcinogenesis. Abstract: In patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), we hypothesize that elevated levels of dietary and circulating linoleic acid initiate a dual mechanism in liver-resident CD4⁺ T lymphocytes. First, linoleic acid directly accumulates in the mitochondria, leading to excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and oxidative damage. Second, the same linoleic acid signal upregulates carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT1), enhancing fatty acid oxidation and further amplifying ROS production. The combined effect of these processes accelerates CD4⁺ T cell apoptosis, thereby compromising tumor immunosurveillance and facilitating the progression of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Advances in high-throughput metabolomics, live-cell imaging, and CRISPR-based gene editing now enable precise quantification of these metabolic shifts and targeted modulation of CPT1 activity or antioxidant pathways, offering novel strategies to restore immune competence and mitigate HCC development.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that elevated linoleic acid in NAFLD upregulates CPT1 in CD4⁺ T cells, leading to apoptosis and reduced tumor immunosurveillance. The new hypothesis retains these fundamental elements but incorporates an additional, well-supported mechanism: direct ROS-induced mitochondrial damage by linoleic acid. This revision acknowledges that linoleic acid induces both ROS generation and CPT1-mediated metabolic reprogramming, creating a synergistic effect that amplifies T cell apoptosis. Furthermore, the revised concept leverages modern technological advances, enhancing its practical implementability and mechanistic clarity.
